vplOperations.details:
The ramp is a list of stops, `elevation:colour`, ascending by elevation in meters, such as `ramp="0:00a000,1000:c8b464,3000:ffffff"`. Between two stops the colour is interpolated linearly, and outside the ramp it is the colour of the nearest end. A colour is `RRGGBB` or, translucent, `RRGGBBAA`; a ramp with a translucent stop gives RGBA tiles, and one without gives RGB tiles. A JPEG source becomes PNG when the ramp is translucent.

Instead of stops, `ramp` takes the name of a ready-made ramp. Each is muted, so that a hillshade on top of it stays legible:

- `default`, the default: a hypsometric tint, shades of blue up to sea level, then green, yellow and brown up to white peaks. Sea level itself is blue, for DEMs that store the sea as 0 m, and so is land below it: `-11000:24507e,-200:8cb4d8,0:bcd8ec,0.01:a8c896,300:cad6a2,800:e4dcae,1500:d6bf98,2500:bea58a,4000:e4e0dc,6000:ffffff`.
- `alpine`: land only, for mountains, from valley green over meadows and brown rock to snow from about 3800 m, and valley green below sea level: `0:a9c39a,500:c6d4a4,1000:dcd9a8,1500:cdbb8f,2000:b7a184,2500:a99c93,3000:cfcbc7,3800:f4f3f1,4500:ffffff`.
- `bathymetry`: sea only, pale blue at the coast to dark blue in the deep sea, and transparent on land, to lie under a ramp for the land: `-11000:0b2545,-6000:13315c,-4000:1d4e89,-2000:3a74b0,-500:6fa3d4,-200:9cc3e6,0:cfe3f3,0.01:cfe3f300`.
- `grayscale`: black in the deep sea, dark grey at sea level and white from 4000 m: `-11000:000000,0:333333,4000:ffffff`.

For a coloured relief, give `dem_hillshade` a `ramp`, which reads and decodes the source once. To draw something between the colours and the shading, stack this under a `dem_hillshade` with `from_stacked_raster`, which lays its first source over the others.

fields.doc: Colour stops, as `elevation:colour,…`, or a ramp name such as `alpine`. Defaults to `default`.
fields.name: ramp

fields.doc: DEM encoding of the source. Defaults to the encoding its tile schema implies.
fields.name: encoding

vplOperations.name: dem_colorize
vplOperations.summary: Colours DEM tiles by elevation, the way MapLibre's `color-relief` layer colours them.

vplOperations.details:
The result is RGBA tiles that are transparent on flat ground and shade slopes by their steepness and the direction they face. They are an ordinary raster source for any map client. Unlike elevation tiles, they can be encoded lossily: with a following `raster_format format=webp quality=70`, a mountain tile at zoom 8 comes out about a quarter smaller than the elevation tile it is computed from, and with `format=avif quality=50` about 60 % smaller. Flat land is the exception: its faint alpha comes out smaller lossless, so for a large area add `lossless_if_smaller=true` to the WebP one, which picks lossy or lossless tile by tile.

The shading is MapLibre's default `standard` method, including the slope exaggeration it applies below zoom 15 and its correction for latitude, so a tile looks as a live `hillshade` layer would at the same zoom. The colours are given as `RRGGBB`, `RRGGBBAA` or `[r,g,b,a]`, and an alpha below `FF` makes that part of the shading lighter.

With a `ramp`, each pixel is the colour for its elevation with the shading drawn over it, which gives a coloured relief in one step. The ramp is written as in `dem_colorize`, which lists the ramps it can name, such as `default`, a hypsometric tint, or `alpine`. A ramp with only opaque stops gives RGB tiles, and a JPEG source stays JPEG; one with a translucent stop gives RGBA tiles, and a JPEG source becomes PNG.

The slopes at a tile's edge are computed with the pixels of the adjacent tiles, so there are no seams. The tiles are read in chunks, several ahead of the ones being shaded, and the edges of every tile are kept for the chunks next to it. Across the antimeridian the neighbour wraps around. Where there is none, at the poles or the edge of the data, the edge pixels are repeated.

fields.doc: Direction the light comes from, in degrees clockwise from north. Defaults to `335`.
fields.name: azimuth

fields.doc: Intensity of the shading, from 0 to 1. Defaults to `0.5`.
fields.name: exaggeration

fields.doc: Colour of slopes facing away from the light. Defaults to `000000`.
fields.name: shadow_color

fields.doc: Colour of slopes facing the light. Defaults to `FFFFFF`.
fields.name: highlight_color

fields.doc: Colour that accentuates steep terrain, such as cliffs and gorges. Defaults to `000000`.
fields.name: accent_color

fields.doc: Colours under the shading, as `elevation:colour,…` or a ramp name. Defaults to none.
fields.name: ramp

vplOperations.name: dem_hillshade
vplOperations.summary: Renders DEM tiles as hillshading, the way MapLibre's `hillshade` layer shades them.

vplOperations.details:
A tile the source has is passed on untouched. A tile it lacks is created from the nearest tile it has at a lower zoom level: the area is cut out and its heights are interpolated up to a full tile, then encoded without loss. This is how a DEM reaches the zoom levels a map asks for when its data ends lower, for a hillshade or contour lines that stay sharp at the edge of the data instead of disappearing.

It is `raster_overscale` for elevation tiles, with the same rules for where tiles are created: inside the source's bounds, up to `level_max`, and never below the source's lowest level. Unlike `raster_overscale`, it always scales heights, never colours, so a source without a DEM tile schema needs `encoding` rather than being scaled as an image; the result carries the tile schema of that encoding.

A following `raster_format` must keep `quality=100`, since a lossy encoder changes the heights.

fields.doc: Highest zoom level to create tiles at. Defaults to the source's highest.
fields.name: level_max

fields.doc: DEM encoding of the source. Defaults to the encoding its tile schema implies.
fields.name: encoding

vplOperations.name: dem_overscale
vplOperations.summary: Creates the DEM tiles a source lacks by upscaling the tiles it has, as heights.

vplOperations.details:
`raster_overview` averages the R, G and B channels independently, which is meaningless for a DEM: the channels are one number split across three bytes, so averaging them separately mixes the high byte of one pixel with the low byte of another. This operation decodes each pixel to its 24-bit raw elevation, averages that, and re-encodes.

Only the averaging differs. Read order, what a tile costs to build on demand, and the memory the intermediate levels use are all as described for [`raster_overview`](#raster_overview).

fields.doc: Zoom level to build the overview from. Defaults to the source's highest.
fields.name: level

fields.doc: DEM encoding of the source. Defaults to the encoding its tile schema implies.
fields.name: encoding

vplOperations.name: dem_overview
vplOperations.summary: Generates lower-zoom DEM overview tiles by averaging 24-bit elevation values.

vplOperations.details:
Discarding low bits that carry no usable signal makes the tiles compress much better. The step is derived per tile from two physical criteria — `elevation_error` relative to the pixel's ground size, and `slope_error` — and the stricter of the two wins. The slope criterion applies to the slope as MapLibre shades it, which exaggerates slopes below zoom 15 (64× at zoom 0).

Values are rounded to the nearest multiple of the step rather than truncated, which halves the worst-case elevation error and removes the downward bias at no cost in size. Single-pass: no scan of the data first.

fields.doc: Allowed elevation error as a fraction of the pixel's ground size. Defaults to `0.1`.
fields.name: elevation_error

fields.doc: Largest slope change in degrees, as MapLibre shades it, quantization may add. Defaults to `1.0`.
fields.name: slope_error

fields.doc: DEM encoding of the source. Defaults to the encoding its tile schema implies.
fields.name: encoding

vplOperations.name: dem_quantize
vplOperations.summary: Quantizes DEM raster tiles by rounding elevations to a per-tile power-of-two step.

vplOperations.details:
The counterpart to `raster_tile_resize` for elevation data: downscaling averages the decoded 24-bit elevation rather than the R, G and B channels separately, which for a DEM would mix the high byte of one pixel with the low byte of another.

The zoom levels shift as in `raster_tile_resize`: splitting moves each tile one level up, except level 0, which is downscaled; merging moves four tiles one level down, so the source's level 0 is not used — level 0 of the result is merged from the source's level 1.

fields.doc: Target tile size in pixels, which must differ from the source's.
fields.name: tile_size

fields.doc: DEM encoding of the source. Defaults to the encoding its tile schema implies.
fields.name: encoding

vplOperations.name: dem_tile_resize
vplOperations.summary: Converts DEM tiles between 256 and 512 pixels by splitting or merging them.

vplOperations.details:
Every parameter narrows the tile set, except `bbox_border`, which widens it. A `bbox_border=2` keeps a ring of tiles the bbox alone would have dropped; those tiles lie outside the crop, so the advertised bounds are extended to cover them and a client actually requests them.

That ring matters wherever a cropped tileset is rendered rather than just stored: without it, labels and geometry near the edge have no neighbouring tiles to be laid out against.

`filename` takes the same path and URL syntax as `from_container`. Opening it to build the allow-list costs I/O when the pipeline is built, unlike every other parameter here.

vplOperations.details:
Left to itself, `max_zoom` picks the level at which the median feature spans roughly 4 tile-pixels, capped at 14. Points count as size zero, so a CSV of points always lands on the cap.

`properties_include` and `properties_exclude` act on what is left after the coordinate and id columns are consumed, so naming `lon_column`, `lat_column` or `id_column` in either has no effect.

A tile over `max_tile_bytes` is dropped while streaming and an error when a single tile is requested. Raise the cap when a legitimate low-zoom tile exceeds it, or set `max_tile_bytes=none` to emit tiles at any size; the soft-cap warning threshold, 200 KB at the default, scales with it.

`bbox` is `[west, south, east, north]` in degrees, and crops while reading: rows outside it are dropped before anything is built, and the tile pyramid is clipped to it. That turns a large CSV into one region's tiles in a single pass, where cropping afterwards with `versatiles convert --bbox` means writing the whole thing out first. The crop is tile-granular, as it is there.

vplOperations.name: from_debug
vplOperations.summary: Generates tiles that draw their own coordinates, for inspecting a pipeline.

vplOperations.details:
### Zoom levels

Unless `level_min` is set, this emits a single zoom level: the dataset's native one. Follow it with [`dem_overview`](#dem_overview) to build the levels below:

```vpl
from_gdal_dem filename="elevation.tif" | dem_overview
```

That is far cheaper than lowering `level_min`. GDAL reads the source at full resolution for every tile it renders, so a low-zoom tile costs as much as all the data it covers, while `dem_overview` builds each tile from the four above it. Use `dem_overview` rather than `raster_overview`, which averages the encoded channels separately and corrupts the elevations.

### Where there is no data

Outside the dataset, outside the cutline and wherever the dataset has its `nodata` value, there is no height, and those pixels are transparent. Their colour is that of 0 m, for readers that ignore alpha. A tile without any data is left out, and a tile the data covers completely has no alpha channel at all.

### Placing an unreferenced raster

A scanned map or a plain image export carries no georeferencing, and GDAL cannot place it at all. `crs` supplies the coordinate system and one of `bounds` or `geo_transform` supplies the position; `crs` on its own is not enough, because a coordinate system says nothing about where the pixels sit.

`bounds` is the north-up shorthand: `west,south,east,north` in the units of `crs` — metres for a projected system, degrees for `4326`. Pixel size is derived from the raster's own dimensions, exactly as `gdal_translate -a_ullr` does, so it cannot disagree with the image.

`geo_transform` takes the six GDAL coefficients verbatim, which is what a rotated or skewed raster needs:

```text
origin_x, pixel_width, row_rotation, origin_y, column_rotation, pixel_height
```

`origin_y` is the fourth number rather than the second, and `pixel_height` is normally negative. `gdalinfo -json` prints this array as its `geoTransform` field, which is the safest thing to copy. World files (`.tfw`, `.wld`) hold the same six values in a different order and measure the origin from the pixel centre rather than its corner, so their numbers cannot be pasted in unchanged.

The two are mutually exclusive, and neither writes anything to the file on disk.

vplOperations.name: from_gdal_raster
vplOperations.summary: Reads a GDAL raster dataset and reprojects it into tiles.

vplOperations.details:
The input format is detected from the file extension:

| Extension                                          | Format                                |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `.geojson`, `.json`                                | GeoJSON `FeatureCollection`           |
| `.ndjson`, `.geojsonl`, `.ndgeojson`, `.geojsonseq` | line-delimited GeoJSON, one feature per line |
| `.shp`                                             | Esri Shapefile                        |

A `.geojsonseq` file may prefix each record with the RFC 8142 record separator `U+001E`.

Input must be **EPSG:4326 lon/lat in degrees, longitude first** — reprojection is not performed. Coordinates outside that range are refused, as is a GeoJSON `crs` member naming another projection, but lat/lon input with the axes swapped is in range and cannot be detected: it produces valid tiles of the wrong place. Reproject first if needed, e.g. `ogr2ogr -t_srs EPSG:4326 out.geojson in.geojson`. A shapefile without a `.prj` is read as WGS84 with a warning, since it carries no CRS of its own.

Left to itself, `max_zoom` picks the level at which the median feature spans roughly 4 tile-pixels, capped at 14. Points count as size zero, so a mostly-point dataset lands on the cap.

A tile over `max_tile_bytes` is dropped while streaming and an error when a single tile is requested. Raise the cap when a legitimate low-zoom tile exceeds it, or set `max_tile_bytes=none` to emit tiles at any size; the soft-cap warning threshold, 200 KB at the default, scales with it.

`bbox` is `[west, south, east, north]` in degrees, and crops while reading: features outside it are dropped before anything is built, and the tile pyramid is clipped to it. That turns a planet-scale extract into one city's tiles in a single pass, where cropping afterwards with `versatiles convert --bbox` means writing the whole thing out first. The crop is tile-granular, as it is there — a boundary tile keeps whatever falls inside it, including the parts of a feature that reach past the box.

`ignore_id` exists because MVT requires a `uint64` feature id. A string id — as USGS earthquake data has — is dropped at encode time anyway, so setting this makes that explicit; it is also the way to discard an id that is just noise.

vplOperations.name: from_geo
vplOperations.summary: Reads a GeoJSON or Shapefile and emits MVT vector tiles.

vplOperations.details:
Gridded statistics are published as a table keyed on a cell id, without the geometry that id refers to. This generates that geometry, so the table can be joined onto it with `vector_update_properties`.

Without GDAL, `epsg` accepts `3035` (ETRS89-LAEA, what European gridded statistics use), `3857` (web mercator) and `4326` (WGS84 lon/lat). A build with the `gdal` feature accepts any code, at roughly ten times the cost per coordinate — and released binaries ship without GDAL, so a `.vpl` naming another code will not run on one.

`bbox` is required: a grid of squares has no extent beyond the one it is given, and in a projected CRS an extent outside the projection's own area is not so much wrong as meaningless.

Within that bbox the grid covers every zoom from the level its cells become legible at up to level 30. Nothing is generated until a tile is asked for, so bound the work where it is done: `versatiles convert --max-zoom`, or a `filter` operation.

`id_template` builds the cell id from literal text and placeholders: `{x}` and `{y}` for the corner, `{epsg}` and `{size}` for the grid's own arguments, each taking an optional divisor (`{x/1000}`), a sign style and a zero-padded width (`{x/100:h04}`). The sign style is `-` for a minus sign when negative (the default), `+` for one either way, `h` for a hemisphere letter — N/S for `y`, E/W for `x` — before the digits, and `H` for one after them.

| Published as | `id_template` |
| --- | --- |
| `CRS3035RES1000mN2691000E4341000` (INSPIRE, the default) | `CRS{epsg}RES{size}m{y:h}{x:h}` |
| `1kmN2689E4337` (GEOSTAT short form) | `{size/1000}km{y/1000:h}{x/1000:h}` |
| `E0643N4567` (CBS Netherlands) | `{x/100:h04}{y/100:h04}` |
| `250mN674400E31725` (Statistics Finland) | `{size}m{y/10:h}{x/10:h}` |

Cell size is fixed by `size` and does not change with zoom — that is what keeps an id stable enough to join against — so low zoom levels are unusable, and the pyramid starts at the level where a tile holds at most `max_cells_per_tile` cells.

vplOperations.details:
The hexagonal counterpart to `from_grid`: data published as a table keyed on an H3 index gets the geometry that index refers to, ready to be joined onto with `vector_update_properties`.

Resolution `0` gives cells of about 4,250,000 km² and `15` about 0.9 m²; `resolution=8` lands near 0.7 km². The full table of cell areas and edge lengths is at <https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/restable/>.

The source covers the whole planet, from the zoom its cells become legible at up to level 30. Nothing is generated until a tile is asked for, so bound the work where it is done instead: `versatiles convert --bbox --max-zoom`, or a `filter` operation.

Cell size is fixed by the resolution and does not change with zoom — that is what keeps an id stable enough to join against — so low zoom levels are unusable, and the pyramid starts at the level where a tile holds at most `max_cells_per_tile` cells. Cells are measured at the equator, where mercator stretches them least, so the level it starts at holds everywhere.

A cell reaching into several tiles is drawn in each of them, clipped to the tile it is in. The same id therefore recurs across tiles, which is what a join expects — but the geometry carrying it in any one tile is only the part inside that tile, so it is not something to measure areas from.

vplOperations.details:
Unlike `from_stacked`, which picks one source's tile whole, this composites them pixel by pixel, so a translucent source lets the ones beneath it show through.

With `auto_overscale=true`, a request that no source covers natively returns an empty stream rather than a blank tile. Put a `raster_overscale` *after* `from_stacked_raster` to fill those in — upscaling one blended tile is cheaper than upscaling each source separately. It fills them up to the highest level any of the sources has, from the nearest level below that has a blended tile.

Elevation sources (tile schema `dem/…`) can be stacked with each other if they all have the same schema; the result keeps it, and is encoded without loss. They cannot be stacked with images, or written as `jpg` or `avif`.

Each of those pairs is mutually exclusive: `tilejson` with `tilejson_file`, `tilejson_update` with `tilejson_update_file`, `vector_layers` with `vector_layers_file`. The `_file` form exists to avoid quoting JSON inline.

Every field the update carries replaces the one below it, including `bounds` and the zoom range — an update that could only widen them would not be able to narrow a tileset's declared extent. Fields the update does not mention are left as they were. `vector_layers` named in the update replace the ones below; layers it does not name are kept.

The fields and their meaning follow the TileJSON 3.0.0 specification: <https://github.com/mapbox/tilejson-spec/tree/master/3.0.0>

vplOperations.details:
The settings apply to every tile that has to be encoded anyway: one in another format, and one that an earlier step of the pipeline created or changed — upscaled, blended, resized, flattened. A tile that is already encoded in the target format is passed through untouched, which costs no time and, for a lossy format, no detail. So `… | raster_overscale | raster_format quality=70 effort=0` encodes the upscaled tiles quickly and leaves the tiles of the source as they are.

Set `force_reencode=true` to re-encode those tiles as well, e.g. to shrink an existing tileset with a lower `quality`.

`quality` and `quality_translucent` take a zoom-dependent list as well as a single number. In `quality="70,14:50,15:20"` the first value is the default and each `zoom:value` pair applies from that zoom level upwards — so zoom 0 to 13 use 70, zoom 14 uses 50, and zoom 15 and above use 20. A value without a zoom applies to the zoom after the previous one: `"70,50"` is 70 at zoom 0 and 50 from zoom 1 upwards. `quality` is ignored for PNG, which is always lossless.

In place of a number, a zoom level can take a range that a quality map chooses from: with `quality="70,16:30-50" quality_map="quality.png"`, zoom 16 and above use 30 where the map is black, 50 where it is white, and an interpolated quality in between. The map is an 8-bit grayscale PNG covering the Web Mercator world, square, with a power of two as its side, so that a pixel is a tile: in a map of 16384 pixels, a tile at zoom 14. A finer tile takes the pixel it lies in. A coarser tile covers several pixels and takes the highest quality any of them gives, so a tile with one white pixel in it is encoded as if it were all white. A plain number ignores the map.

For elevation tiles (tile schema `dem/…`), `quality` defaults to `100`: their channels are heights, and a lossy encoder would change them. `avif` and `jpg` have no lossless encoding, so converting elevation tiles into one of them needs a `quality` for every zoom level.

At a zoom level its list does not name, `quality_translucent` falls back to `quality`. `quality_translucent` is typically `100`: lossy encoders handle an alpha channel badly. Setting it makes every tile that is encoded be checked for opacity.

With `lossless_if_smaller=true`, each tile that is encoded is encoded twice, lossy with its `quality` and lossless, and the smaller of the two is kept. Which one wins depends on the tile, not the zoom level: hillshading of flat land, almost all of it faint alpha, comes out smaller lossless, and that of high relief smaller lossy. In a sample of the planet's hillshading at zoom 10 to 12, `quality=70 lossless_if_smaller=true` took 59 % of the bytes of `quality=70` alone, and the tiles came out lossless nine times out of ten. Encoding takes about 1.7 times as long. It needs `format=webp`, the only format that has both a lossy and a lossless encoding. A tile whose quality is `100` is encoded lossless only, once.

With `invert=true` the pixels inside it become transparent instead, which cuts a hole into the map:

```vpl
from_container filename="satellite.versatiles" | raster_mask geojson="city.geojson" invert=true
```

The buffer always grows what stays visible, so inverted, a positive buffer shrinks the hole and a negative one widens it. The blur band stays where it is, its ramp reversed.

The mask is not reprojected: coordinates outside the WGS84 range are refused, as is a `crs` member naming another projection. A mask written lat,lon is in range and cannot be detected — it masks the wrong part of the world.

Overlapping polygons in the GeoJSON are merged first, so an area covered twice stays inside.

vplOperations.name: raster_mask
vplOperations.summary: Makes raster pixels outside a GeoJSON polygon transparent.

vplOperations.details:
A tile the source has is passed on untouched. A tile it lacks is created from the nearest tile it has at a lower zoom level: the area is cut out and scaled up. The result is blurry rather than detailed — the point is that every tile up to `level_max` has an answer, from the best data there is at that place. For a source with worldwide imagery at its low levels and aerial imagery for some regions on top, that fills in everything between.

Tiles are only created inside the bounds of the source, so set them with `meta_update bounds=…` in front if they are missing or too wide. A tile that would be completely transparent is not created; a transparent tile the source has is passed on like any other. Nothing is created below the source's lowest level.

Elevation tiles are scaled as heights, not as colors, and encoded without loss. They are recognised by the tile schema of the source, `dem/mapbox` or `dem/terrarium`; set it with `meta_update schema=…` in front if the source does not declare it. A source with the schema `dem/versatiles` is refused: its tiles cannot be scaled as heights. `dem_overscale` does the same for elevation tiles only, and takes the encoding as a parameter instead.

A source whose bounds are the whole world is filled for the whole world, which is fine for serving and far too many tiles to write to a file at a high `level_max`.

The tiles created are encoded with the encoder's own settings, which aim at keeping detail these tiles do not have: at the default quality a created WebP tile is as large as one of the source's, and most of the time it takes to create goes into encoding it. Put `raster_format` behind this operation to change that, e.g. `raster_format quality=75 effort=0`. It reaches the created tiles only; the tiles of the source keep their bytes. Not for elevation tiles: a quality below 100 changes their heights.

fields.doc: Highest zoom level to create tiles at. Defaults to the source's highest.
fields.name: level_max

vplOperations.name: raster_overscale
vplOperations.summary: Creates the raster tiles a source lacks by upscaling the tiles it has.

vplOperations.details:
Every zoom level is built from the four tiles above it, down to zoom 0. Read depth-first — which is what a conversion does, unless the destination insists on another order — each tile is built exactly once.

Any other order produces the same tiles, at a different price. Tiles are built a 16x16 block at a time, so one tile at zoom `z` built from a cold start costs `256 * 4^(level - z)` source tiles — bounded by however many the source actually has under it, which for anything short of global coverage is far fewer. The block is not waste: its neighbours come out of it for free.

The consequence is that the first request into a region of a dense, deep pyramid is expensive and the rest are not. Over a zoom-14 world, one cold zoom-6 tile reads some sixteen million source tiles; over a city-sized source, the same request reads a handful. Serving a dense deep pyramid live is therefore not what this is for — convert once, serve the result.

Writing `.pmtiles` is the same situation, because that format stores tiles in an order this cannot produce for free; it succeeds, and says in the log what it is costing.

Levels are held in memory between being built and being consumed, within `VERSATILES_OVERVIEW_CACHE_MB` megabytes (default `2048`).

fields.doc: Zoom level to build the overview from. Defaults to the source's highest.
fields.name: level

vplOperations.name: raster_overview
vplOperations.summary: Generates the lower zoom levels of a raster pyramid by downscaling.

vplOperations.details: Changing the tile size shifts the zoom levels with it, because the ground resolution of a pixel has to stay the same. `tile_size=256` splits each 512-pixel tile into four 256-pixel tiles one zoom level higher, except at level 0, which has no level below it to move to and is downscaled instead. `tile_size=512` merges four 256-pixel tiles into one 512-pixel tile one zoom level lower, so the result ends one level below the source. The source's level 0 would have to move to level −1 and is not used: level 0 of the result is merged from the source's level 1, the same area in more detail.

fields.doc: Target tile size in pixels, which must differ from the source's.

vplOperations.details:
The three flags are applied in a fixed order — `flip_x`, then `flip_y`, then `swap_xy` — and between them reach all eight symmetries of the square: four rotations and four reflections, which is every relabelling that maps the tile grid onto itself. Because that set is closed, chaining two of these operations is never necessary; some single combination of the three flags does the same thing.

The combinations most likely to be wanted:

| `flip_x` | `flip_y` | `swap_xy` | result                    |
| -------- | -------- | --------- | ------------------------- |
| false    | true     | false     | TMS ↔ XYZ row order       |
| false    | false    | true      | `z/y/x` ↔ `z/x/y` layouts |
| true     | true     | false     | rotate 180°               |
| true     | false    | true      | rotate 90°                |

Unlike a global `--flip-y` flag, this applies to one source, so a pipeline can combine sources that disagree about their conventions.

fields.doc: Whether to mirror horizontally, so `x` becomes `2^z - 1 - x`. Defaults to `false`.
fields.name: flip_x

fields.doc: Whether to mirror vertically, so `y` becomes `2^z - 1 - y`. Defaults to `false`.
fields.name: flip_y

fields.doc: Whether to exchange the axes, so `(x, y)` becomes `(y, x)`. Defaults to `false`.
fields.name: swap_xy

vplOperations.summary: Relabels tile coordinates, correcting a source that uses TMS row order or `z/y/x` paths.

vplOperations.details:
The features for which `expr` is true go through the first source, the `then` branch. The others go through the second, the `else` branch, or pass through unchanged when there is none. Both halves are then put back together into one tile, with the features of each layer in their original order.

```vpl
from_container filename="osm.versatiles"
  | vector_branch expr="$layer == 'place_labels'" [
      vector_mask geojson="berlin.geojson"
    ]
```

That cuts the place labels to Berlin and leaves every other layer as it was.

`expr` is written as in `vector_filter_features`, with names such as `$zoom`, `$layer`, `$type` and `$props` beside the feature's own properties; see there for the full list. It is answered for as much of a tile at once as it can be: an expression reading only `$zoom`, `$x` and `$y` sends each tile to one branch without decoding it, and one that also reads `$layer` but nothing of the feature sends whole layers.

A branch begins with a transform rather than a read, because it starts from the tiles arriving here. It may only contain operations that make each tile from that tile alone, such as filtering, masking or changing properties. An operation that reads other tiles, such as `vector_overzoom`, is refused; put it before or after the branch.

Branches nest, which is how to write an "else if". This keeps motorways in Germany, other streets in Berlin, and everything else everywhere:

```vpl
from_container filename="osm.versatiles"
  | vector_branch expr="$layer == 'streets' && kind == 'motorway'" [
      vector_mask geojson="germany.geojson",
      vector_branch expr="$layer == 'streets'" [
        vector_mask geojson="berlin.geojson"
      ]
    ]
```

### Sources

vplOperations.name: vector_branch
vplOperations.summary: Runs part of each vector tile through other operations, chosen by an expression.

vplOperations.details:
The expression is evaluated for every feature of every layer. Most filters are written for one layer, so they go in a `vector_branch` that hands that layer over and leaves the others as they are:

```vpl
from_container filename="osm.versatiles"
  | vector_branch expr="$layer == 'place'" [
      vector_filter_features expr="name == 'Berlin'"
    ]
```

The same in one expression is `$layer != 'place' || name == 'Berlin'`, which keeps every feature of the other layers. The branch costs less, because it hands over whole layers without evaluating the expression for each of their features.

### Examples

The examples below show the operation on its own, as it would stand inside such a branch:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="name == 'Berlin'"
vector_filter_features expr="population >= 1000"
vector_filter_features expr="highway in ['primary','secondary']"
vector_filter_features expr="name.matches('^St\\.')"
vector_filter_features expr="name != null && name != ''"
vector_filter_features expr="$props['addr:street'] == 'Hauptstr.'"
```

### Expression language

`expr` is a boolean [CEL (Common Expression Language)](https://github.com/google/cel-spec) expression, evaluated once per feature.

**Types** — bool (`true`, `false`), int / uint (`42`, `-7`, `1000u`), double (`3.14`, `-0.5`, `1e-6`), string (`'hello'` or `"hello"`), list (`[1, 2, 3]`, `['a', 'b']`), map (`m['key']` or `m.key`), and `null`.

**Operators** — equality `==` `!=`, ordering `<` `<=` `>` `>=`, logical `&&` `||` `!`, membership `x in [1, 2, 3]`, and `s.matches('pattern')` for a regex in RE2 syntax, matched anywhere in `s`.

### Accessing feature properties

Properties whose names are valid CEL identifiers — letters, digits and underscore — are exposed as top-level variables:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="name == 'Berlin'"
```

For keys containing `:`, `-`, `.`, or anything else that is not an identifier, use the `$props` map:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="$props['addr:street'] == 'Hauptstr.'"
```

### Names starting with `$`

Some names describe a feature and where it is rather than the properties it carries. They start with `$`, which no property name can, so they never collide with one:

- `$zoom` — the zoom level of the tile being filtered, as an integer.
- `$x` and `$y` — the column and row of that tile, as integers.
- `$layer` — the name of the feature's layer, as a string.
- `$type` — the feature's geometry type: `'Point'`, `'LineString'` or `'Polygon'`, as in MapLibre's `geometry-type`, or `null` if the tile does not say. A tile does not tell one point from several, so a multipoint is `'Point'` too.
- `$id` — the feature's id, as an integer, or `null` if it has none.
- `$props` — all of the feature's properties, as a map.

`$type` and `$id` are stored beside the feature's geometry, so reading them does not decode it.

`$zoom` lets one expression keep different features at different zooms — which is how cartography actually reads a layer:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="kind in ['motorway','trunk'] || $zoom >= 12"
```

That keeps motorways everywhere and every other street only from z12. An expression that reads only `$zoom`, `$x` and `$y` is answered once per tile, and one that also reads `$layer` once per layer, rather than once per feature, so a plain zoom range is cheap:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="$zoom >= 14"
```

The bare words `zoom` and `props` are refused, because they meant `$zoom` and `$props` before the `$` was required. A feature property of either name is `$props.zoom` or `$props.props`. So are `_zoom`, `_x`, `_y`, `_layer`, `_type`, `_id` and `_props`, which are reserved because the names starting with `$` are read through them. Any other property, including ones named `layer`, `type`, `id`, `x` or `y`, is a bare identifier as usual.

### Missing keys

A property a feature does not carry resolves to `null` for identifier-safe access, so compare against `null` to say explicitly whether such features are kept or dropped:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="name != null && name != ''"
```

The `has()` macro asks the same question of an identifier-safe key, and `in` of any key:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="has($props.name)"
vector_filter_features expr="'addr:street' in $props"
```

### Evaluation failures

A feature is kept only when the expression evaluates to `true`. An expression that fails to evaluate, or that returns something other than a boolean, drops the feature — there is no separate error channel per feature, so a filter that cannot be answered filters nothing in.

The common way to reach that is an ordering comparison against a property that is absent or is not a number:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="population >= 1000"
```

A feature with no `population` compares `null` against a number and is dropped. Guard the comparison to say so deliberately:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="has($props.population) && $props.population >= 1000"
```

Equality and membership are safe without a guard: `==`, `!=` and `in` compare across types and return `false` rather than failing. Ordering comparisons — `<` `<=` `>` `>=` — are the ones that fail, and a `has()` guard does not rescue a property that is *present* but holds a string, because `&&` short-circuits only on `false`.

`is_num(x)` closes that gap. It asks whether a value is a number and answers rather than failing, so an ordering comparison can be made total:

```vpl
vector_filter_features expr="is_num($props.population) && $props.population >= 1000"
```

This is an extension rather than standard CEL, added because there is no other way to write the guard — `type()` does not exist here, and `int()` and `double()` answer by failing, which costs exactly what the guard was meant to avoid.

Besides comparisons, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `? :` and arithmetic, an expression can call the functions `size`, `max`, `min`, `string`, `int`, `uint`, `double`, `bytes` and `is_num`, the methods `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith` and `matches`, and the macros `has`, `all`, `exists`, `exists_one`, `map` and `filter`.

The [CEL language spec](https://github.com/google/cel-spec/blob/master/doc/langdef.md) has the full grammar. It also lists functions this build does not have, such as `timestamp`, `duration` and `type()`.

vplOperations.details:
Points outside the polygon are dropped, and lines and polygons are cut at its edge. A point exactly on the edge counts as inside. Properties are kept as they are.

```vpl
from_container filename="osm.versatiles" | vector_mask geojson="berlin.geojson"
```

Every layer is cut, and tiles outside the polygon are not produced at all. To cut only some layers, put the mask in a `vector_branch`. This keeps place names inside the region while country and state names stay on the whole map:

```vpl
from_container filename="osm.versatiles"
  | vector_branch expr="$layer == 'place_labels'" [
      vector_mask geojson="berlin-brandenburg.geojson"
    ]
```

With `invert=true` it keeps what lies outside the polygon instead, exactly what is dropped without it: a point or line on the edge is dropped, and so are the tiles the polygon covers. This leaves a hole for an overlay:

```vpl
from_container filename="osm.versatiles" | vector_mask geojson="city.geojson" invert=true
```

Tiles entirely on the kept side pass through without being decoded, and tiles entirely on the other side are dropped without being decoded, so only tiles on the edge are. Geometry in a tile's buffer is cut where it really lies, up to one tile beyond the tile's edge.

Cut geometry is rounded back to the tile grid, and a sliver that rounding collapses is dropped.

The mask is not reprojected: coordinates outside the WGS84 range are refused, as is a `crs` member naming another projection. Overlapping polygons in the GeoJSON are merged first, so an area covered twice stays inside.

fields.doc: Path or URL of a GeoJSON file holding a Polygon or MultiPolygon, in EPSG:4326 lon/lat degrees.
fields.name: geojson

fields.doc: Whether to keep what lies outside the polygon instead of what lies inside. Defaults to `false`.
fields.name: invert

vplOperations.details:
A tile the source has is passed through unchanged. A tile above the source's highest level is clipped out of the source's tile at that level and its coordinates rescaled. No detail is added — the geometry is the parent's — but a client can keep zooming instead of hitting a blank map. A tile that would hold no features is not created.

Nothing is created at or below the source's highest level, and nothing from a tile further down: a vector tile the source lacks is a place with nothing in it. To overzoom from a lower level than the source's highest, put `filter level_max=…` in front.

`level_max` has to be set, and above the source's highest level: left out or lower, the operation has nothing to do and is refused. Each extra level quadruples the tile count.

fields.doc: Highest zoom level to serve, capped at `30`. Defaults to the source's highest, which is refused.
fields.name: level_max

fields.doc: Clip buffer in tile-extent units, so edge-straddling features survive. Defaults to `80`.

vplOperations.details:
Always fixed: missing `extent` and `version` fields, duplicate layer names, inverted polygon winding, and degenerate rings.

Tiles the validator considers clean pass through unchanged — the original encoded blob is forwarded without re-encoding — so this operation is cheap on conformant input.

Without `drop_offenders`, a layer holding a feature whose geometry cannot be decoded keeps its original geometry bytes, while the structural fixes are still applied to it.

### Example

```vpl
from_container filename="bad.versatiles" | vector_repair
from_container filename="bad.versatiles" | vector_repair drop_offenders=true
```
